summary: Gives an overview of telephone number portability in the Global Switched Telephone Network, where users keep their numbers when changing providers. This turns a dialed number from a physical routing address into a virtual one, requiring translation before calls can be routed.

eli5.summary: People like keeping their phone number when they switch companies. This note explains how that works and why phone systems must look numbers up before connecting calls.

subtitle: How customers keep their phone numbers when changing carriers

tldr.problem: Telephone numbers were originally tied to physical locations and carriers, making it expensive and inconvenient for customers to switch service providers. This barrier to competition motivated regulatory changes.
tldr.mechanism: Number portability separates a dialed number (virtual address) from the network routing address through a translation database, allowing customers to keep their number while the routing changes. Different schemes handle this translation at different points in the call path.
tldr.outcome: Service provider number portability (SPNP) is now widely deployed in North America, Europe, and other regions, enabling customer choice and competition in local telephony markets. The RFC provides an overview of how different countries implement this infrastructure.

today: RFC 3482 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains a valuable overview of number portability concepts and global implementation approaches. Service provider number portability is now standard in most countries with competitive telecommunications markets.

sections.title: What Number Portability Is
sections.content:
This RFC gives an overview of E.164 number portability (NP) in the Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN). Historically, telephone numbers were physical routing addresses: the digits you dialed told the network which physical switch at which carrier served that line. If you changed carriers, you had to accept a new number because you were now served by a different switch.

Number portability changes this. It lets customers keep their phone number when they switch service providers. To make this work, the network separates the dialed number (now a virtual address) from the actual routing address. When a call arrives for a portable number, the network queries a database to find where that number has moved, then routes accordingly. This shifts regulatory power from carriers to customers.

Three types of NP exist: geographic number portability (GNP) for fixed and mobile numbers, non-geographic number portability (NGNP) for special numbers like 800 services, and mobile number portability (MNP) for wireless subscribers.
sections.eli5: Your phone number used to mean "you are at this carrier." Number portability makes it mean "you belong to this person, wherever they go." The network has to look up your real location every time someone calls.

sections.title: Types of Portability
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes several categories. Service Provider Number Portability (SPNP), also called operator portability, lets you keep your number when changing carriers. Location portability lets you keep your number when you move to a new physical location. Service portability lets you keep your number when upgrading from basic telephone service to ISDN or roaming between networks.

The document focuses on SPNP because it has been the primary regulatory driver. Historically, local telephone service was regulated as a utility and was not competitive. As countries began liberalizing their markets (around 1995 onwards), SPNP became a requirement to prevent customers from being locked into a provider.
sections.eli5: There are different kinds of portability. The main one is letting you keep your number at a new carrier. Another lets you keep it at a new address. A third lets you keep it when upgrading your service type.

sections.title: Four Routing Schemes
sections.content:
The RFC describes four standardized schemes for how networks route calls to ported numbers:

All Call Query (ACQ): The originating network queries a centralized database immediately for every call to a potentially portable number, gets back the new routing address, and routes the call directly to the new carrier. This is most efficient because it avoids querying the old carrier.

Query on Release (QoR): The originating network first tries the old carrier's network. When the old carrier detects the number is ported out, it releases the call and indicates this. The originating network then queries the database and routes to the new carrier.

Call Dropback (Return to Pivot): The originating network routes to the old carrier, which queries its own internal database, detects the ported-out status, and releases the call back with the new routing address. The originating network then initiates a new call to the new carrier.

Onward Routing (OR): The originating network routes to the old carrier, which queries its own database and routes the call directly to the new carrier. This requires two physical call segments and is the least efficient in circuit usage.
sections.eli5: Four methods exist. One asks a central database right away. One tries the old carrier first, and only asks the database if needed. One has the old carrier look it up and send the call back. One has the old carrier complete the routing to the new carrier.

sections.title: Databases and Call Routing
sections.content:
Different regions use different technologies to query the Number Portability Database (NPDB). In North America, carriers use protocols including Advanced Intelligent Network (AIN), Intelligent Network (IN), IS-41 for wireless, GSM MAP for PCS systems, and ISUP triggerless translation (which queries in the signaling layer itself).

In Europe, operators use ITU-TS Intelligent Network Application Part (INAP) Capability Set 1 or 2 to query databases. Wireless networks in Europe often use internal databases at the donor switch rather than centralized ones.

For call routing, North America uses a Location Routing Number (LRN): a ten-digit number assigned to each switch that currently serves ported numbers. The NPDB returns the LRN, and the originating network routes to that address. Europe uses routing prefixes (short codes prepended to the dialed number) or separate routing parameters to achieve the same goal. Different countries use different prefix formats and coding schemes.
sections.eli5: Different regions built different systems to look up numbers. North America uses a special ten-digit routing address. Europe adds a prefix to the original number. Both work, but they had to build them separately because there is no international number portability.

sections.title: Global Implementation Status
sections.content:
The RFC documents the status of NP deployments worldwide as of 2003. Many countries have implementations: the United States uses ACQ with LRN routing, Canada uses similar schemes, and Australia deployed NP in 1999-2000. European countries vary: the UK uses onward routing, Spain and Germany use ACQ, Belgium uses a hybrid approach. Various other countries including Austria, Denmark, Finland, France, Italy, Japan, and Sweden have their own implementations.

The RFC also notes number pooling, an enhancement used in the U.S. to conserve scarce area codes. Instead of assigning whole phone number ranges (CO codes) to a carrier's switch, pooling allows multiple carriers to share a single range, with the NPDB determining which carrier actually serves each individual number within that range.
sections.eli5: By 2003, many countries had set up their own versions. Each chose different technical approaches based on their existing networks and rules. The US system, Europe's systems, and others all work but are incompatible across borders.
